It is also said that the meaning is "a man" from two men of the two towns. The man from Makkah was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and it is said he was Utba ibn Rabi'a. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 33:

﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community⁠—﴾ etc.: This is also a belittling of this world. Its meaning: Were it not that all people would disbelieve, We would have given to the disbelievers roofs of silver, and this is because of the worthlessness of this world before Allah, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If this world were worth the wing of a gnat in the sight of Allah, He would not have given a disbeliever a single sip of water from it." ﴿And stairways by which they would ascend﴾. Al-ma'arij (stairways) means the ramps and ladders; the meaning of yazharun (they would ascend) is they would rise up, and from it comes "fa-ma istata'u an yazharuhu" (so they were not able to scale it). Al-surur is the plural of sarir (couches), and al-zukhruf is gold. It was also said that it is the household furnishings of curtains, cushions and the like. And it was said: it is gilding, carving and similar adornment, like His saying: ﴿until, when the earth takes on its adornment and becomes beautiful﴾ [Yunus: 24].

﴿Whoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil﴾. *Ya'shu* comes from your saying *'ashiya al-rajul*, when a man's sight grows dim. Here it means darkness of the heart and of insight.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *yaʿshā*, with a fatha on the shin, is used when an affliction has befallen the eyes, while *yaʿshū*, with a damma on the shin, is used when one looks like a *aʿshā* (one with weak sight) without there being any affliction. The difference between them is like the difference between your saying *ʿamiya* (he was blind) and *taʿāmā* (he feigned blindness). So the meaning of the reading with the damma is: he feigns ignorance and denies his knowledge of the truth. The apparent meaning is that this is an expression for heedlessness and neglecting to reflect.

﴿The remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾: Al-Zamakhshari said that it means the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAtiyya said that it means what God has mentioned to His servants of admonitions. In that case the verbal noun is attributed to its agent. In my view it may also mean the servant's remembrance of God.

The meaning of the verse is that whoever is heedless of the remembrance of God, God facilitates for him a devil who becomes his companion. That is a punishment for heedlessness toward remembrance, by empowering the devil over him, just as whoever persists in remembrance, the devil keeps far from him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 37:

﴿And indeed they (the devils) turn them away from the way﴾. The pronoun in "innahum" (indeed they) refers to the devils, and the object pronoun in "yasuddunahum" (they turn them away) refers to the one who turns away (ya'shu) from the remembrance of the Most Merciful. The two pronouns are in the plural because the intended meaning is plural.

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾. Naafi', Ibn Katheer, Ibn 'Aamir and Abu Bakr read "jaa'anaa" with the dual pronoun, referring to the one who turns away and his devil. The rest read it without the alif, as a single pronoun referring to the one who turns away (man ya'shu). The pronoun in "qaala" (he says) is in ﴿And whoever turns away (ya'shu)﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 36], and it is said that it refers to the devil.

﴿The distance of the two easts﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first is that it means the east and the west, and one of them was given precedence in the comparison, as it is said "al-qamarayn" (the two moons, meaning the sun and the moon). The second is that it means the two easts and the two wests, and "the two wests" was omitted because "the two easts" indicates it.

This is a statement said to the disbelievers in the Hereafter, and its meaning is that their sharing in the punishment will not benefit them, nor will they find the comfort of consolation that the afflicted person finds in this world when he sees another suffering the same as what has afflicted him. The subject of "yanfa'akum" (will benefit you) is the clause ﴿أَنَّكُمْ فِي ٱلْعَذَابِ مُشْتَرِكُونَ﴾ (that you are, in the punishment, sharers). "Idh zalamtum" (when you did wrong) is a causal clause, meaning: because of your wrongdoing. It has also been said that the subject is an implied element, namely the disavowal (al-tabarri') which is required by his saying: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts" (Qur'an 43:38), and in that case "annakum" would be read as a causal particle. The first view, however, is more preponderant.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verses 40–41:

﴿Then can you make the deaf hear?﴾ etc. This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant by "the deaf and the blind" is the disbelievers, since they did not comprehend the proofs of Islam. ﴿So whether We take you away, indeed We will take vengeance upon them﴾. The word "fa-imma" (so whether) is composed of "in" (the conditional particle "if") and the superfluous "ma". The purpose of the verse is a threat to the disbelievers. The meaning is: if We hasten your death before taking vengeance upon them, We will indeed take vengeance upon them after your death; and if We delay your death until the time of taking vengeance upon them, We are indeed capable over them. This vengeance may be intended to mean their killing on the day of Badr, the conquest of Makkah, and similar vengeance in this world, or it may be intended to mean the punishment of the Hereafter. It is also said that the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to the Muslims, and that the meaning of this is that Allah decreed that He would take vengeance upon them through trials and hardships, and that He honoured His Prophet, peace be upon him, by causing him to die before seeing the vengeance upon his community. The first view is more well-known and more evident.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 44:

﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. The pronoun in ﴿innahu﴾ refers either to the Qur'an or to Islam. The word *dhikr* (reminder) here means honour (*sharaf*), and the people of the Prophet ﷺ are the Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs, for they attained, through Islam, the honour of this world and the Hereafter. It suffices as proof that they conquered the eastern and western regions of the earth, and that caliphate and kingship came to be among them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that authority after him would belong to the Quraysh. It is also possible that *dhikr* means admonition and exhortation, in which case "his people" (*qawmuhu*) on this reading are all of his community and everyone to whom he was sent. ﴿And you will be asked﴾, i.e., you will be questioned about acting upon the Qur'an and about thanking Allah for it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 45:

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers﴾ If it is said: How was the Prophet ﷺ commanded to ask the earlier messengers when he did not meet them? The answer is in three aspects. The first: he saw them on the night of the Isra'. The second: the meaning is "ask the community of those whom We sent before you." The third: he did not intend actually asking them; rather the meaning is that their laws agree upon the Oneness of God, such that if they were asked, "Is there any god worshipped besides God?", they would deny that and profess Oneness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 48:

﴿And We did not show them any sign except that it was greater than its sister.﴾ The "signs" (al-ayat) here are the miracles, such as the staff turning into a serpent and the hand coming out white. It has also been said that they are the proofs and rational arguments, but the first view is more apparent. The meaning of "greater than its sister" is that it is at the utmost degree of greatness and clarity. It does not mean that it is preferred over other signs; rather the meaning is that when one looks at it, one finds it great, and when one looks at other signs, one finds them great too. This is like the saying of the poet:

Whomever of them you meet, you will say, "I have met their chief," — like the stars by which the night traveler is guided.

This is what al-Zamakhshari said. However, in my view it is possible that he means: no sign of Ours that We showed them was except that it was greater than what came before it. So the intended meaning is "greater than its sister" in the sense of the preceding sister sign.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 43, verse 49:

﴿And they said, "O sorcerer, invoke for us your Lord"﴾. The apparent meaning of their words is a contradiction. Their saying, ﴿O sorcerer﴾, implies their denial of him, while their saying, ﴿invoke for us your Lord﴾, implies their affirmation of him. The answer is in two ways. The first is that those who said this were deniers, and their saying ﴿invoke for us your Lord﴾ means according to your claim and your assertion. Their saying ﴿indeed, we will be guided﴾ is a promise they intended the opposite of. The second is that they were affirmers, and their saying "O sorcerer" either is not blameworthy in their view, because sorcery was the knowledge of the people of their time, and it is as if they said, "O scholar," or it is a title they had become accustomed to using for Moses from the very beginning when he came to them, so they uttered it afterward without believing in its meaning.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 51–52:

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾ It is possible that he called out to them himself, or that he ordered a herald to proclaim among them. ﴿He said: "O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me﴾ He intended by this to boast over Moses. Misr (Egypt) is the well-known city and what belongs to it, and its extent runs from the branch of Alexandria to Aswan along the length of the Nile. ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ meaning: the great canals branching out from the Nile flowed beneath his palace, and the greatest of them are four rivers: the river of Alexandria, Tinnis, Damietta, and the river of Tulun. ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ The view of Sibawayh is that the particle أم (am) here is connected and equivalent (muttasilah mu'adilah), and the meaning is: "Will you not see, or do you not see?" Then he placed his words ﴿I am better﴾ in the place of "you see," because when they say to him "you are better," they are, in his estimation, people with sight; this is the placing of the cause in the place of the effect. The original would have been to say: "Will you not see, or do you see?" Then he confined himself to أم and omitted the verb after it, and resumed with his words ﴿I am better﴾ in the manner of a statement. It is also stopped upon at this word (أم), but this is weak. It has been said that أم here means بل (bal), so it is disjunctive (munqati'ah). ﴿...better than this one who is contemptible﴾ ﴿and who can hardly express himself clearly﴾ This points to what remained in Moses' tongue from the effect of the live coal, for it had produced a knot in his tongue; when he prayed that it be loosened, his prayer was answered, but there remained from it a trace which stayed with him as a slight impediment (lukna). It has also been said that it means a stammer (ayy) in speech. His words ﴿and he can hardly express himself clearly﴾ imply that he did express himself clearly, because "kada" (يكاد), when negated, implies affirmation.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verses 54–56:

﴿So he made his people feel foolish, and they obeyed him﴾ — meaning he sought to make them light-minded by this statement and captivated their minds. ﴿They angered Us﴾ — meaning they provoked Our wrath.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 43, verse 57:

﴿When the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas and others in his tafsir (exegesis) of this verse that when the mention of Jesus son of Mary and the praise of him were revealed in the Qur'an, the Quraysh said: "Muhammad only wants us to worship him, just as the Christians worshipped Jesus." This was their aversion from citing him as an example. Ibn Atiyya related this. The one who cited the example here is God, in the Qur'an. The word "yasuddun" (يَصِدُّونَ) means "they turn away" (يُعرضون).

Al-Zamakhshari said: When the Messenger of God ﷺ recited to the Quraysh, "Indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell" [al-Anbiya: 98], they were offended by this. Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bara said: "Is this specific to us and our gods, or to all nations?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is for you and your gods, and for all nations." He said: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'ba! Do you not claim that Jesus son of Mary was a prophet, and praise him highly? You know that the Christians worshipped him. If Jesus is in the Fire, then we are content for us and our gods to be with him." The Quraysh rejoiced at this and laughed, and the Prophet ﷺ remained silent. Then God the Exalted revealed: "Indeed, those for whom the best reward from Us has preceded, they will be kept far away from it" [al-Anbiya: 101], and this verse was revealed.

According to this view, the meaning is: when Ibn al-Za'bara cited Jesus as an example and argued with the Messenger of God ﷺ about the Christians' worship of him, the Quraysh, from this example, "yasuddun", that is, they laughed and cried out with joy. This meaning fits the reading "yasiddun" (يَصِدُّونَ) with a kasra on the sad, meaning clamour and shouting (الضجيج والصياح).

﴿And they say: "Are our gods better, or is he?"﴾ They mean by "he" Jesus. The meaning is that they said: "Are our gods better, or Jesus? If Jesus is to enter the Fire, then we are content to be, we and our gods, with him, since he is better than our gods." This statement is a completion of what came before it, according to what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his tafsir of the preceding verse. As for what Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned, this is the beginning of another meaning. Al-Zamakhshari related another opinion regarding the meaning of this verse: that when they heard the mention of Jesus, they said: "We are more rightly guided than the Christians, for they worshipped a human being, while we worship the angels." They said, "Are our gods, who are the angels, better than Jesus?" Their aim was to prefer their gods over Jesus. It was also said: their saying "or is he" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), for when they said, "Muhammad only wants us to worship as the Christians worshipped Jesus," they said, "Are our gods better, or is he?", intending to prefer their gods over Muhammad (ﷺ). The more apparent view is that "he" refers to Jesus, and this is the view of the majority. This is indicated by the earlier mention: ﴿They did not strike this example for you except for argument﴾, i.e., they did not put forward this example to you except as a matter of dispute (jadal), which is that a person intends to overcome the one who debates him, whether he overcomes him with truth or with falsehood. For Ibn al-Za'bara and those like him, it was not hidden that Jesus was not included in the Almighty's words "the fuel of Hell" (ḥaṣab jahannam), but they wanted to deceive (mughalata), so God described them as a people given to contention (khiṣam).

﴿He was only a servant upon whom We bestowed favor﴾ — meaning ʿĪsā (ʿalayhi al-salām), and the favor upon him was prophethood, the miracles, and other things besides.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 60:

﴿And if We willed, We would have made among you angels to succeed one another upon the earth.﴾ Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: "If We willed, We would have made in your place angels who would dwell on the earth and succeed the children of Adam in it." So his saying "minkum" (from you) is connected either to the omitted "badal" (substitute), or to "yakhlufun" (they succeed). The second: "If We willed, We would have made from you," i.e., "We would have begotten from you children who are angels, who would succeed you on the earth just as your children succeed you. For We are able to create angels from the offspring of people. So do not deny that We created 'Isa without a father." This is related from al-Zamakhshari.

Verse 43:61: ﴿And indeed, it is a sign (ʿilm) for the Hour﴾. The pronoun refers to Jesus, and it was also said to refer to Muhammad (ﷺ), and it was said to refer to the Qur'an. As for the view that it refers to Jesus or to Muhammad, the meaning is that it is one of the signs of the Hour, which necessitates knowledge of it, so the sign was called ʿilm because knowledge of it is attained through it. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiyallahu ʿanhu) read ﴿لَعَلَم﴾ with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and the lam, meaning a sign (ʿalāma). As for the view that it refers to the Qur'an, the meaning is that it informs you about the Hour.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 63:

﴿And so that I may make clear to you some of that about which you differ; so be mindful of God﴾. It has also been said that "some" (baʿḍ) here means "all" (kull), but this view is weak.

Its meaning: God will say on the Day of Resurrection to the righteous, "O My servants, no fear shall be upon you today, nor shall you grieve."

The other said: "He hears our private conversation but does not hear our secret." ﴿Their secret and their private conversation﴾: the secret (sirr) is what a person speaks to himself or to others in secret, and the private conversation (najwa) is what they speak among themselves. ﴿Yes [indeed]﴾, meaning We do hear, and Our messengers with that are writing down what they say; the messengers here are the angels who guard the deeds.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 81:

﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of the worshippers.﴾ In its interpretation there are four opinions. The first is that it is an argument and a refutation directed at the disbelievers, on the supposition of their statement, and its meaning is: If the Most Merciful had a son, as the disbelievers say, I would be the first to worship that son, just as the servants of a king venerate the king's son out of honour for his father. But the Most Merciful has no son, so I worship none but Allah alone. This is a type of proof called dalil al-talazum (the proof of necessary implication), because it ties the worship of the son to his existence, and since his existence is impossible, his worship is impossible. The second opinion: If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first to worship Allah alone, and I would be refuting your claim that He has a son. According to these two opinions, al-'abidin (the worshippers) is taken in the sense of worship. The third opinion: al-'abidin is taken in the sense of those who deny, as it is said, "'abida al-rajul" when a man becomes disdainful and proud and rejects something. The meaning then is: If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first to deny that. The conditional particle "in" (if) is conditional according to these three opinions. The fourth opinion, related by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd, is that "in" here is a negation, meaning "The Most Merciful did not have a son," and the speech is complete; then a new statement begins: ﴿So I am the first of the worshippers﴾. The first opinion is the correct one, because it is a well-known method in proofs and arguments, and it is the one relied upon by al-Zamakhshari. Al-Tabari said: it is a courteous manner of address (mulatafat al-khitab), and similar to it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance or in manifest error﴾ [Saba': 24]. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: from it is the saying of the Exalted in addressing the disbelievers: ﴿Where are My partners?﴾ [al-Nahl: 27], meaning, My partners according to your claim.

"And it is He who is God in the heaven and God on the earth." Meaning: He is the God for the people of the earth and the people of the heaven. The prepositional phrase (al-majrur, "in the heaven" and "on the earth") is connected to "God" (ilah), because it carries the sense of a qualifying description.

"And with Him is the knowledge of the Hour." Meaning: the knowledge of the time of its occurrence.

"And those whom they call upon besides Him do not possess intercession." Meaning: no one who is worshipped besides Allah possesses the ability to intercede with Allah, because no one intercedes with Him except by His permission; so He alone is the owner of intercession.

"Except those who testify to the truth while they know." Scholars differed over whether this means that the one who testifies to the truth is the intercessor or the one for whom intercession is made. If it means the one for whom intercession is made, then the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and the meaning is: the objects of worship do not possess intercession; but whoever testified to the truth while knowing it is the one for whom intercession is made. On this reading it is possible that "those who testified" is the object of the verb "intercession" with the preposition dropped, its sense being: intercession for those who testified to the truth. If by "those who testified to the truth" is meant the intercessor, then the exception may be disjunctive or may be connected (muttasil), the connected reading being: except those who worshipped Jesus and the angels. The meaning on this reading is: the objects of worship do not possess intercession, except for those who testify to the truth.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 43, verse 88–89:

﴿And [He knows] his saying, "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾ The word "qīl" (qīl) is a verbal noun like "qawl" (saying), and the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also read as "qīlahu" (qīlahu) in the accusative and genitive, and in readings outside the seven canonical ones it is read in the nominative. As for the accusative, it is said that it is conjoined to "sirrahum wa-najwāhum" (their secret and their private counsel), and it is said that it is conjoined to the position of "al-sāʿah" (the Hour), since that is an object governed by a verbal noun that has been put in construction; and it is said that it is conjoined to an omitted object, its implied sense being: "they write down their sayings and his saying." As for the genitive, it is said that it is conjoined to the wording of "al-sāʿah" (the Hour), and it is possible that it is conjoined to His saying "bi-l-ḥaqq" (with truth). As for the nominative, it is said that it is the subject (mubtada') and what follows it is its predicate. Al-Zamakhsharī weakened all of that and said: it belongs to the category of oaths, so the accusative and genitive are by suppressing the oath particle, as when you say: "By Allah, I will surely strike Zayd," and the nominative is like their saying: "Aymanu Allāh" (By the rights of Allah) and "laʿamruka" (by your life). The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are a people who do not believe﴾, as if he said: "He swears by his saying that these are a people who do not believe." ﴿So turn away from them﴾ — abrogated by the sword. ﴿And say, "Peace"﴾ — its implied sense is "my affair is peace," i.e., conciliation; and it is said it means "peace be upon you," in the manner of disengagement, and it is abrogated in both interpretations. ﴿But they will come to know﴾ — a threat.
